title: Philly-Style Cheesesteaks
shortDescription: Chopped ribeye, melted provolone, soft hoagie
subtitle: Chopped ribeye, melted provolone, soft hoagie
description: Philadelphia-style cheesesteaks for the hall: shaved ribeye chopped on the flat-top, sweet onions, and provolone melted straight into the meat so it binds every bite on a soft hoagie. Sized for a full crew, with timing that still works when the kitchen gets interrupted.
equipment: Flat-top griddle or two large cast-iron skillets
Two stiff metal spatulas or bench scrapers

ingredients.name: Ribeye, Shaved Or Sliced Paper-Thin
ingredients.notes: partially freeze 30 min, until firm but not frozen solid, for easy slicing; sirloin works on a budget

ingredients.name: Provolone Slices
ingredients.notes: deli provolone or white American — the melty kind

ingredients.name: Soft Hoagie Rolls Or Brioche Buns
ingredients.notes: long Amoroso-style hoagies are classic; soft round brioche rolls work too — just never a crusty baguette

steps.title: Chill and shave the ribeye
steps.instruction: Partially freeze the ribeye for 30 minutes, until firm but not frozen solid, then shave or slice it paper-thin against the grain — thin is what makes a cheesesteak tender instead of chewy. If your grocer or butcher sells pre-shaved ribeye, buy it and skip this. Keep the meat cold until the griddle is ripping hot.

steps.title: Sweat the onions low and slow
steps.instruction: Slice onions thin. Cook in 1 tbsp oil over medium 12–15 minutes, stirring, until soft, golden, and sweet — not raw-sharp and not burnt. Push to the cool side of the griddle or pull to a pan and hold warm. Sweet onions are the balance against the salty beef and cheese.

steps.title: Optional peppers and mushrooms
steps.instruction: For a 'wit peppers' or mushroom crew, sauté the sliced bell peppers and mushrooms in a little oil over medium-high until soft and lightly charred, 8–10 minutes. Season with a pinch of salt and hold warm alongside the onions. Skip entirely for a purist build.

steps.title: Sear the ribeye hard, in batches
steps.instruction: Get the flat-top or cast iron screaming hot and film with oil. Lay the shaved ribeye down in batches — a crowded surface steams the meat gray instead of browning it. Season with salt and pepper. Let it catch color 60–90 seconds before you touch it.

steps.title: Chop and pile the meat
steps.instruction: Work the beef with two stiff spatulas or bench scrapers, chopping it into short shreds as it browns to an internal temp of 145°F or above. Fold the warm onions (and peppers/mushrooms if using) into the meat and gather it into portion-sized piles on the griddle — about 6 oz of meat per sandwich.

steps.title: Melt the cheese into the meat
steps.instruction: Lay provolone over each pile — about 1.5 slices per sandwich — and let the residual heat melt it into the beef so the cheese binds the shreds together. That melt-in, not melt-on, is the whole trick to a real cheesesteak. Cover with a lid or foil tent for 30 seconds to speed it if the griddle has cooled.

steps.title: Warm the hoagie rolls
steps.instruction: Split soft hoagie rolls most of the way through and warm them cut-side down on the griddle just until barely toasted and warm — soft, not crunchy. A crusty roll fights the filling; a warm soft roll cradles it.

steps.title: Bake steak fries (optional)
steps.instruction: Spread frozen steak fries in a single layer on sheet pans. Bake at 425°F 22–25 minutes until deeply golden with an audible crunch when shaken. Salt immediately out of the oven; hold in a warm oven with the door cracked.

steps.title: Scoop, fill, and run the line
steps.instruction: Use the spatulas to scoop each cheese-bound pile straight into a warm roll — flip it in so the cheese side lands against the bread. Set fries on a separate tray so steam doesn't sog the rolls, and call the crew while the cheese is still molten.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-cook, scrape the chopped ribeye into a hotel pan, cover, and hold at 140°F or above in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — the thin meat dries fast, so ladle a spoon of its own juices over top and don't hold past 30 minutes without re-saucing. Melt cheese and fill rolls to order when you're back so the bread never goes soggy.

steps.title: Pack down leftovers safely
steps.instruction: Cool the chopped cheesesteak meat in shallow hotel pans within two hours — deep pans hold heat too long. Label with the date; reheat to 165°F on a hot griddle with a splash of water before second shift. Store rolls separately and fill fresh so they don't turn to paste.

proTips: Partially freeze the ribeye for 30–45 minutes, until firm but not frozen solid, before slicing — paper-thin meat is the difference between tender and chewy.
Melt the provolone into the meat pile, not onto the finished sandwich — melted-in cheese glues the shreds together the way a real cheesesteak should.
Keep the griddle ripping hot and work in batches; a crowded surface steams the beef gray instead of browning it.
Warm the rolls soft, never crunchy — a crusty roll pushes the filling out the back on the first bite.
Sirloin sliced thin is a fine budget swap for ribeye; season a little harder since it's leaner.
tonightSpread: Main: Philly-style cheesesteaks with provolone melted into the meat
Sides: steak fries, sweet griddled onions
Condiments: optional peppers and mushrooms, extra provolone, hot cherry peppers
Set hot components closest to the crew; cold crunch and toppings at the far end of the line.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run.
leftovers: Cool the chopped cheesesteak meat in shallow pans within two hours; label with date and reheat to 165°F before second shift.
Store rolls separately and fill fresh — toasted rolls go soggy overnight.
Reheat the meat on a hot griddle with a splash of water so it steams back to juicy instead of drying out.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Chopped ribeye, melted provolone, soft hoagie — the Philly build every crew recognizes. One griddle, real portions, no drama at the stove.
substitutions: Ribeye ↔ thin-sliced sirloin — leaner and cheaper; season a little harder.
Provolone ↔ white American for a smoother melt, or warmed cheese sauce for a Whiz-style build.
No flat-top? Two large cast-iron skillets over high heat do the same job in batches.

adaptable.label: Gluten-Free Adaptable
adaptable.note: Use a certified gluten-free bun/bread and toast on a separate, clean surface. Use a certified gluten-free frozen fry/tot brand, or fresh-cut potatoes.

adaptable.note: Use a dairy-free cheese shred/block alternative.
